entries.title: Taiwan flags improper treatment by China during APEC meetings
entries.paragraph_1: The official said Taiwan had initiated discussions with China soon after Beijing was selected as the host of the APEC meetings in November 2024. The negotiations were aimed at ensuring Taiwan's equal participation as a member economy, while also securing the safety and freedom of movement of its delegates during the events. According to the Central News Agency, Taipei and Beijing conducted 17 rounds of negotiations between November 2024 and the conclusion of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday. Taiwan also approached like-minded countries to seek diplomatic support and raise concerns over its treatment during the meetings. However, despite these efforts, Taiwan encountered several difficulties. The official said Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin was prevented from attending the APEC Small and Medium Enterprises Ministerial Meeting held in Guangzhou in September, with China citing political reasons for its decision. The official also raised concerns over the manner in which Taiwan's invitation to the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting was delivered, as well as its format. Although further details were not disclosed, Taiwan had reportedly urged Beijing to follow the arrangements adopted in 2014, when China last hosted the APEC summit, including having a Chinese official personally deliver the invitation. However, Beijing did not meet Taiwan's expectations on the matter, the official said, as reported by the Central News Agency. Despite the developments, Taiwan maintained that China's actions would not establish a precedent for future APEC meetings. The official emphasised that the incidents would not alter Taipei's position on securing equal treatment and participation in the regional economic forum. Meanwhile, more than 400 Taiwanese representatives from over 25 government ministries and agencies travelled to China this year to participate in APEC-related meetings at different levels, highlighting the scale of Taiwan's engagement with the forum, the Central News Agency reported. (ANI)

entries.title: SKNVibes | Global Security Has No Room for Blind Spots: Why Taiwan Belongs in INTERPOL
entries.paragraph_1: For island nations like St. Kitts- Nevis and Taiwan, the sea is not a barrier—it is a vital artery connecting us to the world. Yet in an era of hyper-connectivity and borderless digital technology, those same global networks are increasingly exploited by transnational criminals. From sophisticated cyber-fraud syndicates and cryptocurrency laundering to international narcotics trafficking, crime knows no borders. Unfortunately, global law enforcement remains handicapped by a glaring blind spot: the political exclusion of Taiwan from the International Criminal Police Organization (INTERPOL).
entries.paragraph_2: Founded in 1923, INTERPOL’s mandate under Article 2 of its Constitution is clear: to “ensure and promote the widest possible mutual assistance between all criminal police authorities.” Despite this mission, Taiwan has been barred from the organization for over four decades due to Beijing’s deliberate distortion of United Nations General Assembly Resolution 2758. By conflating UN representation with Taiwan’s participation in specialized bodies, China has obstructed Taiwan’s engagement across the international system. Only Taiwan’s democratically elected government has the legitimacy to represent its 23.5 million people—and when Taiwan is silenced, partners around the globe, including across the Caribbean, pay the price.

entries.paragraph_2: Quattordici a cinque. Quattro anni fa, alle elezioni locali del 2022 , il risultato era stato questo. Delle 22 cariche principali in palio alle cosiddette 九合一 (“ nove in uno “, per il fatto che si vota per nove categorie di cariche locali), circa due su tre erano andate al Kuomintang (KMT) e meno di un terzo al Partito Progressista Democratico (DPP), coi restanti tre posti al Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) e a un candidato indipendente. Si era pochi mesi dopo la visita di Nancy Pelosi a Taipei e il DPP (al governo dal 2016) ottenne il peggior risultato di sempre al voto locale. Quattro anni dopo, tutti e tre i partiti con rappresentanza parlamentare hanno cambiato volto: la leadership è di Lai Ching-te e non più di Tsai Ing-wen, a guidare il KMT c’è Cheng Li-wun e non più Eric Chu, il TPP ha perso il suo leader Ko Wen-je a causa di guai giudiziari. Non cambia il fatto che il voto è visto come un test rilevante in vista delle elezioni presidenziali e legislative, distanti “solo” 14 mesi. Non si può sottolineare mai abbastanza quanto il voto locale abbia logiche proprie, in ampia parte scollegate a temi strategici o alle questioni delle relazioni intrastretto, ma è innegabile che funzioni come innesco degli equilibri in vista del voto di gennaio 2028, anche e soprattutto per quanto può accadere all’interno dei partiti. Stavolta, peraltro, la corsa per la guida di Taipei consegnerà in ogni caso un risultato importante per due figure con evidenti ambizioni che vanno oltre la poltrona di sindaco della capitale.

entries.title: Historic China-Russia-US summit delivers a heavy blow to 'Taiwan independence' forces - China Military
entries.paragraph_1: A view of the Taiwan Straits is seen from Xiamen port, in East China's Fujian Province. Photo: IC
entries.paragraph_2: Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a summit in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province on Thursday. Both the Russian and US leaders expressed their appreciation to China for hosting the historic summit. The three heads of state had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security. China particularly underscored the importance of "not challenging the red lines of one another." On the same day, during his bilateral meeting with President Xi, President Trump explicitly reiterated the US position of not supporting "Taiwan independence." All these important signals, taken together, deliver a heavy blow to "Taiwan independence" separatist forces on the island. The Taiwan question is at the very core of China's core interests. It is the first red line that must not be crossed in any country's relations with China. For a long time, "Taiwan independence" separatist forces have repeatedly tested the limits of danger because they have clung to the illusion that they can exploit tensions between major powers, seeking to profit from the rivalry among them. But with the leaders of China, Russia and the US sharing a common understanding on safeguarding world peace and reaching a series of important consensuses on strategic stability and international security, the logic on which these separatists have long relied - that they can "exploit divisions among major powers" - is being fundamentally undermined. The geopolitical cracks they have hoped to exploit are steadily closing. Containing "Taiwan independence" separatist forces has become a matter of shared understanding and common interests among major powers. For the US, allowing "Taiwan independence" forces to cross red lines would mean facing the risk of a military confrontation that could spiral out of control at any moment. For Russia, upholding the post-World War II international order and opposing "Taiwan independence" in any form have long been consistent positions. For China, eradicating the "Taiwan independence" scourge is an inevitable requirement for achieving the complete reunification of the country. For major powers such as China, Russia and the US, a Taiwan Straits crisis deliberately provoked by "Taiwan independence" separatist forces serves none of their fundamental interests. In other words, any attempt to seek narrow political gains by fomenting division and provoking conflict will be seen by major powers alike as a direct threat to strategic stability. As consensus among major powers continues to strengthen, China has both the capability and the resolve to steadily squeeze the space of "Taiwan independence" forces through a comprehensive range of political, economic, military and legal measures, until they are no longer capable of taking action. When "Taiwan independence" that once was seen as a card by certain external forces becomes a hot potato or even a liability that undermines stable relations among major powers, it will only be a matter of time before "Taiwan independence" is discarded like a worn-out shoe. The encirclement of "Taiwan independence" separatist forces will only tighten. What awaits them is a reckoning and the condemnation of history.

entries.title: Nvidia Chip Packaging Deal Funds SPIL Lines Making AI Chip Interposer Wafers, Not Just Assembly
entries.paragraph_1: Nvidia is funding new production lines at Taiwanese chip-packaging company SPIL that cover bumping, interposer wafer fabrication , assembly and testing, according to the agreement Nvidia announced Tuesday. An interposer is the silicon routing layer that connects an AI processor to its memory stacks. Making interposers has typically been TSMC's CoWoS front-end step , so the scope points to Nvidia financing a second source for part of the front half of an AI chip package, not only more back-end floor space. Neither company has said how the interposers will be made or under what license.
entries.paragraph_2: Nvidia released the multiyear agreements at 5:18 p.m. ET Tuesday, naming six partners: Amkor, Foxconn, Kinsus, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL and TSMC. SPIL said Wednesday in Taiwan that it will triple its advanced packaging capacity there by mid-2029, and Nvidia described its funding as multibillion-dollar without giving a figure.
